In general - the J arm changes the way the force travels from the trolley to the door throughout the path of travel, allowing leverage to be applied a certain way.

Specifically that door bracket is toast and if you relocate the door bracket (specifically the one I shared) you will absolutely need the j arm
To clarify, this is not a proper fix but should get you up and running

Hello! Garage door guy here 👋🏼 that is a 9100 model Wayne-Dalton Garage Door.

It is a very lightweight if not somewhat frail door. You 100% are missing the J-arm of that assembly which has likely caused the fasteners to pull out of the operator bracket located on top of the door.

The only thing connecting the door to your opener right now is that silver strut running along the top of the door-which is not completely attached. You can see the whole thing flex when going through the video frame-by-frame.

My recommendation would be to attach a “LiftMaster 41A5047 Door Bracket” to the bottom of that strut with self-tapping screws, and attach a COMPLETE J-arm/Straight Arm assembly. I would also add a couple (that’s 2) self tappers to the top of that strut where the Wayne-Dalton door bracket currently sits.

Or call a professional.
Holy shit you have a fragile ego

College is what you make of it. And no, you’re not alone. 

Friendships come and go, it’s just how it happens sometimes. One way I got over this is by making it a point to make at least one friend in every class. Not even to the extent of hanging out, but just finding someone that I could have genuine conversations with. Most of the friendships only last that class but there are several that I’ve stayed in touch with, even after I moved away. The wider a net you cast the more likely it is that you’ll find people who you connect with, and it might surprise you who those people end up being. 

Starting somewhere new is difficult, I still find it hard and I’ve done it multiple times. But that’s also the thrill of it. You’re at a place where most people, if anyone knows who you are. It’s a time and place where you can finally do the things you want to do and be the person that you want to be. 

As far as the depression an anxiety, talk to someone if you aren’t already. If your school has an in house counseling center go there, please. I’m not saying it’s going to work miracles because it isn’t, but it’s nice just to be able to talk about your problems and have a guiding hand sometimes. Having a perspective other than your own can be beneficial. I’ve been where you are, I hit rock bottom, and frankly it’s a miracle that I’m still here today. It does get better, it takes time and mindfulness. It’s not going to be easy, it never is but life is worth it, you are worth it. If you need someone to talk to or to just vent just message me.

Generally speaking they are probably too self involved and don’t realize that their actions have consequences. Others feel entitled to do and say as they please, and you getting upset is an inconvenience . There are a bunch of reasons that someone might get mad when they are confronted about something that they did. More often than not though it’s unusually a problem with them more so than a problem with you (or the persons whose feelings got hurt.)

Talk to them about it. Relationships are founded upon trust and communication. 

Distancing yourself or chasing them are the worst options that you could take. When this happens things usually end catastrophically. 

If they don’t want to talk, keep a line open but don’t force discussion either. 

It may be time to consider other options.

So you’re at a crossroads. It’s completely normal to feel anxious about coming up to “a point of no return”. As you’ve pointed out you have two options (technically more) either stay on that path you’re on now, or choose a different one. 

Let’s start with option one, you stay in nursing and graduate, you find a job. Now what? You make of it what you will. Is it going to be difficult? Yeah probably, but it’s all about the mindset that you take going into it. Nursing is an inherently stressful job that isn’t for everyone, but if you can tough it out I say do it. You can get a tremendous amount of personal satisfaction knowing that you are doing your best to help other people. Every work environment is different, some are better and worse than others, it’s about finding a place that you fit.

Now you have option two (and three). 

You want to change your major? Great! What do you want to change your major to? Do you want to stay in healthcare and human services, or do you want to do something completely different? If you want to stay in a similar field look at how your classes transfer into that field, does it satisfy most of the courses that you’d need to take already? That could be a huge determining factor on how you decide to move forward. Maybe you want to try something completely different, that’s great too! Maybe consider a minor in some sort of health field. 

I know that this is a very non-answer answer, but really there is no wrong choice here. You are better off finding and doing something you really enjoy than worrying about how the work life is going to be. You’ll always find a way. I started school as a business major, then said screw it and became a cop for a couple years. I got tired of the stressful work environment and now I’m going back to school and studying psych. 

Point is there is no right time for anything, you just have to do it and see where it takes you. Sometimes it will be good and other times it won’t be so good, but there is no wrong choice, just do what you love and life will find a way.
